what_it_does: Training a science-specialized AI model requires parsing millions of research papers stored as PDFs, but the highest-quality parsing tools process only 1-2 PDFs per second — far too slow to build trillion-token datasets in any reasonable time. AdaParse solves this by automatically routing each PDF to the cheapest parser that will produce good enough output, using a cascade of lightweight classifiers, so that most documents get parsed instantly by a fast tool and only the genuinely difficult ones go to the expensive AI-powered parser. The result is 17x higher throughput at equivalent or slightly better accuracy.
method_in_detail:
The idea. Not all PDFs are equally hard to parse. A clean, born-digital paper from a recent conference can be read accurately by a fast text extraction tool (PyMuPDF) in milliseconds. A scanned document with complex equations may require a large vision-based AI model (Nougat, a 350-million-parameter transformer that converts page images to text) that takes seconds per page. The key insight is that using Nougat on everything is wasteful, but using the fast tool on everything produces garbage for complex documents. The right answer is to triage: identify which documents need the expensive parser and send only those.

How it works. AdaParse implements a three-stage filter.

Stage 1 (CLS I — Validity Check): PyMuPDF is first run on every document. This is 135x faster than Nougat. The extracted text is checked with simple rules (character count, presence of garbled characters, etc.). If the text looks completely invalid, the document is sent directly to Nougat. If it looks fine, it moves to Stage 2.

Stage 2 (CLS II — Improvement Likelihood): Metadata about the document (authoring software, publication year, number of pages) is fed into a regression model that predicts whether a better parser would meaningfully improve the output. If improvement is unlikely, PyMuPDF's output is accepted as-is. If improvement is likely, Stage 3 runs.

Stage 3 (CLS III — Parser Selection): The extracted text itself is fed into a fine-tuned version of SciBERT (a language model pre-trained on scientific text) that classifies which parser among several options is best for this specific document. This fine-tuning uses a technique called Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) — instead of training on a fixed accuracy metric like BLEU (a measure of word-sequence overlap), the model is trained on actual human preferences collected from 23 domain experts across mathematics, biology, chemistry, and other fields, who rated pairs of parser outputs for the same page.

The key design choice. DPO alignment makes the parser-selection model optimize for what scientists actually prefer, not just what automated metrics reward. Human experts agreed with each other 82% of the time, validating that preferences are objective enough to train on. Importantly, the preferences are collected once offline — no human input is needed at deployment time.

Parallel execution on a supercomputer. The Parsl workflow library orchestrates execution across the Polaris supercomputer at Argonne National Lab. Nougat's model weights are kept warm across tasks (loaded once, reused for many documents) to avoid 15-second reload delays. PDFs are batched into compressed archives and loaded into node-local RAM to avoid hammering the shared filesystem.

The result. AdaParse achieves 78 PDFs/second on 128 nodes versus Nougat's 8 PDFs/second — a 17x throughput improvement — while achieving 0.2% better BLEU score than Nougat alone, because AdaParse sometimes routes documents to other parsers that outperform Nougat on those specific documents.
